transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CISO - StratusBank), Ethan Morales (Cloud Infra Eng), Lena Voss (Compliance Manager)
Recorded: yes

[00:00] Sofia Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sofia, I'm the account lead on the private deployments team at Redwood. With me is Daniel Park, our technical SE. Um, we'll do a quick run of the architecture and then dive into network and key management controls.
[00:20] Priya Rao: Hi all, Priya here. We're specifically concerned around network ingress/egress controls, how keys are managed when data at rest and in transit, and the audit log paths into our SIEM. Also need to validate SOC2 controls for our regulators.
[00:34] Daniel Park: Great, thanks. Quick show of hands — is everyone comfortable with seeing the architecture diagram? We shared the PDF in the calendar invite (arch-diagram.pdf). If not I can screen share.
[00:43] Ethan Morales: I have it open, thanks.
[00:45] Lena Voss: Got it.
[00:46] Daniel Park: Cool. So at a high level the private deployment is a control plane that we operate, and the customer runs the data plane inside their VPC — or optionally on-prem. The control plane talks over a dedicated management channel, we support AWS VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, and for on-prem we've got an appliance package that can be air-gapped.
[01:10] Priya Rao: Clarify — you say "control plane we operate" — are you saying Redwood still has any external ingress to our VPC? We need zero internet ingress for regulated workloads.
[01:20] Sofia Chen: Good question. For strict zero-internet setups we can do a private control plane that connects over an outbound-only TLS tunnel initiated from your side, or we can deploy the entire control plane inside your VPC if you opt for the on-prem / VPC-bundled package. So by default we avoid inbound ports; everything can be client-initiated out to a private endpoint.
[01:41] Ethan Morales: So you'd prefer we open minimal egress to your management IPs, is that right? We would need to lock that to a small CIDR or PrivateLink.
[01:50] Daniel Park: Yes, you can either restrict egress to our advertised PrivateLink endpoint or create a VPC endpoint and route through it. For private link there's no public internet path. For the outbound TLS tunnel option we publish a set of IPs and FQDNs — you can restrict via security groups and egress rules.
[02:05] Priya Rao: Can you list the exact TCP ports and protocols we need? Our firewall team needs explicit rules.
[02:10] Daniel Park: Absolutely — typical is TCP 443 for control plane TLS. For metrics/heartbeat we use a separate port over TLS as well (443 on a separate path). If you enable model fetching from our curated model catalog there may be additional egress to S3-compatible endpoints for model blobs — that can be routed through PrivateLink/S3 VPC endpoint. I'll include an exact port/protocol table in the doc we send.
[02:32] Lena Voss: What about certificate management — where does TLS terminate? We don't want Redwood terminating TLS interior to our VPC.
[02:39] Sofia Chen: For VPC-native we recommend TLS termination at the customer ALB — we support mTLS between the ALB and the data plane containers if you want mutual TLS. For the control plane interface when we host it, TLS terminates at Redwood's ingress, but all data plane traffic within your VPC is under your control. If you require full end-to-end TLS we can also enable TLS passthrough.
[03:05] Ethan Morales: mTLS — what's required from our side? Certificates and a PKI?
[03:10] Daniel Park: You can bring your own certs via ACM (if in AWS) or we can accept a PKCS12 bundle. For on-prem you can use your PKI and rotation policies. We also support integration with Vault for dynamic cert issuance.
[03:22] Priya Rao: KMS — we need to ensure keys are under our control and HSM-backed. Do you support customer-managed KMS keys?
[03:30] Daniel Park: Yes, we support customer-managed CMKs in AWS KMS with key policies that explicitly grant the service principal limited decrypt/encrypt usages. For HSM-backed keys we can integrate with CloudHSM and bring-your-own-HSM workflows. For on-prem we have an HSM connector that keeps private key material inside your boundary.
[03:46] Lena Voss: How are keys rotated and audited? We need a record of key use in our audit logs.
[03:52] Daniel Park: Key usage events are written to the KMS audit trail (CloudTrail or your equivalent). We also emit an internal Redwood audit event for each decryption operation which can be forwarded to your SIEM over syslog or to S3/bucket endpoints with KMS-encrypted objects. We'll show mappings to SOC2 control points in the doc.
[04:10] Priya Rao: Audit logs retention — we have a 7-year retention for certain records. Can you support long-term storage?
[04:17] Sofia Chen: Yes — logs can be exported to your S3 with lifecycle policies or forwarded to your SIEM. We don't persist PII in Redwood-managed buckets by default for private deployments; your retention controls dominate.
[04:30] Ethan Morales: On the network diagram I see a NAT gateway in the public subnet for egress — is that required? We want to avoid public NAT for data plane egress.
[04:40] Daniel Park: Not required. The NAT is an optional pattern we show for convenience. For strict isolation we recommend PrivateLink and VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, and other services, and use VPC endpoint routing to keep traffic internal. We can also recommend using a service firewall or egress proxy inside your private subnet.
[04:58] Priya Rao: Firewalling — will Redwood provide any recommended L7 rules or IPS signatures?
[05:03] Daniel Park: We provide recommended security group and NACL templates. For L7 WAF/IPS we integrate with existing WAF providers via ALB or Gateway APIs — we don't ship a bundled IPS by default, but our on-prem appliance can be fronted by your WAF. We can also front traffic through an Envoy sidecar to enforce mTLS and RBAC at the service layer.
[05:25] Ethan Morales: Envoy sidecar — does that introduce latency? We have strict P50 latency targets.
[05:30] Daniel Park: Minor added latency (few ms) depending on configuration. We can run perf benchmarks in your environment during the PoC. We also offer selective sidecar for the control plane only, not the token path, to minimize impact.
[05:42] Priya Rao: RBAC and SSO — can you integrate with our SAML provider and SCIM for provisioning? We need role separation and audit trail for admin actions.
[05:52] Sofia Chen: Yes, we support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning. Roles map to Redwood RBAC constructs; admin actions are logged with actor identity and can be sent to your audit collector. We support conditional access (IP restrictions) through SAML assertions.
[06:08] Lena Voss: Is there an option for hardware-backed attestation for hosts? We want to verify nodes are untampered for on-prem.
[06:15] Daniel Park: For on-prem we can integrate with TPM-based attestation and supply a shim that verifies host integrity at boot. For cloud we integrate with Nitro attestations where available (AWS Nitro).
[06:28] Ethan Morales: Data residency — our VPC is in eu-west-1 and we must ensure no data leaves region. How do you enforce regional residency for model artifacts and logs?
[06:38] Sofia Chen: For private deployments we run everything inside the region you pick. Control plane metadata can be restricted to the region or run in your VPC if you choose the full private control plane. Model artifacts can be stored only in region-specific S3 or artifact storage; we can add a guardrail that prevents cross-region replication.
[06:55] Priya Rao: SOC2 — do you have a current Type II and can you share the report under NDA?
[07:00] Sofia Chen: Yes, we have a SOC2 Type II for our hosted and private offerings. We'll share the redacted report and the control matrix under NDA. I'll attach the SOC2 summary to the follow-up.
[07:10] Lena Voss: Encryption in transit — you said at ingress TLS 1.2+? We require TLS 1.3 preferred, and perfect forward secrecy.
[07:16] Daniel Park: We support TLS 1.3 and PFS. We can require TLS 1.3 for all endpoints in your deployment.
[07:23] Ethan Morales: How about secrets management for service accounts? We want short-lived credentials and rotation integrated into our Vault.
[07:29] Daniel Park: We support Vault integration and OIDC-based short-lived tokens. Our agents can request ephemeral credentials from your Vault via the transit backend; we don't require long-lived static secrets.
[07:40] Priya Rao: For audit events — do you push canonical JSON events or syslog? Our SIEM prefers JSON over HTTPS inbound.
[07:48] Sofia Chen: We can stream events in JSON to an HTTPS collector, push via syslog, or write to an S3 bucket. We'll sketch the options in the integration guide.
[07:58] Ethan Morales: IDS/IPS — do you provide alerts or do we need to manage that entirely?
[08:04] Daniel Park: We can emit telemetry and suggested alerting rules; typically customers run their own IDS/IPS. For on-prem we can optionally run Suricata signatures and forward alerts to your SIEM.
[08:14] Priya Rao: Regulatory review — can you map Redwood controls to NIST/ISO/SOC2 for our audit team?
[08:21] Sofia Chen: Yes, we maintain a control mapping matrix: SOC2, ISO 27001 mappings, and NIST CSF. We'll include the mapping doc and call out any shared responsibilities.
[08:32] Lena Voss: Shared responsibility — can you summarize what the customer must own vs Redwood? We're often asked to produce a statement for our auditors.
[08:40] Sofia Chen: Sure. Short version: Redwood owns the Redwood-managed control plane and its operational security. Customer owns VPC network controls, keys if you bring CMKs, host hardening if on-prem, and perimeter firewall rules. We'll provide a templated SR statement you can include in your evidence kit.
[08:58] Ethan Morales: Logging latency — when you forward logs to our SIEM, are they batched? What's the expected delay?
[09:05] Daniel Park: Typically sub-minute for events; most customers see 10-30s. For very high-volume telemetry we batch to reduce cost; audit-critical events are forwarded immediately.
[09:16] Priya Rao: Can you demonstrate the log line for a decryption operation? We need an example for our logging policy.
[09:22] Daniel Park: Yep — I'll paste an example in the doc, it includes timestamp, requestor principal, action (Decrypt), resource ARN, result (Success/Failure), and correlation ID.
[09:31] Sofia Chen: Quick callout on egress: for model downloads we can host artifacts in your S3 to avoid outbound to Redwood blob stores. That's often the simplest way to maintain residency.
[09:42] Ethan Morales: That works.
[09:43] Priya Rao: Any background checks or personnel controls we should be aware of for teams with access to customer environments?
[09:49] Sofia Chen: We have background check policies for engineers with access to infra, documented in the SOC2 pack. We can provide specifics for staff that will be assigned to your account under NDA.
[09:59] Lena Voss: What about penetration testing — can our security team run pen tests against the on-prem appliance?
[10:05] Daniel Park: We allow customer-initiated tests on the customer-side of the deployment; for Redwood-managed control plane tests we require coordination and a scope of work. We'll provide approved test windows and coordinates.
[10:18] Priya Rao: Thank you.
[10:20] Sofia Chen: Great. To wrap up, let's capture the concrete next steps: we'll send the SOC2 summary, architecture PDF with explicit port list, and a private deployment checklist; you (Ethan) will send the current firewall/egress whitelist and Lena will confirm logging retention. Then we'll schedule the PoC network test.
[10:38] Ethan Morales: Sounds good.
[10:40] Lena Voss: OK.
[10:41] Sofia Chen: Anything else before we close?
[10:43] Priya Rao: One last question — pricing impacts for dedicated private deployments and any premium support for compliance audits?
[10:49] Sofia Chen: We'll include a pricing sketch in the follow-up and the support add-on for audit assistance.
[10:55] Daniel Park: I'll put together the firewall rules, PrivateLink examples, and a terraform snippet to provision endpoints.
[10:59] Sofia Chen: Thank you everyone — we'll follow up by Friday with the docs.
[11:02] Priya Rao: Thanks, bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional overlap between Priya and Ethan; some product names transcribed as "redwood control plane" vs internal shorthand. Certain technical tokens sometimes spelled out (e.g., K-M-S as letters) due to audio.

References mentioned during call:

- SOC2_TypeII_redacted.pdf (to be shared under NDA)
